Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The handshape on the last sign was clear, and I could follow the whole sentence. My one note is that your eyebrows stayed raised through the next phrase too, so I wasn't sure where the question ended. Could you try a little pause there?

Rowan: thanks, that helps. I was trying to remember the question marker and i think i just kept my eyebrows up while i searched for the next sign. I'll watch it again tonight and see if a pause makes the boundary easier to read.

Jules: The pause sounds worth testing, but don't make it so long that it looks like you forgot the sentence. In our study group, we use a small breath as a reminder to reset our face, not a full stop every time.

Rowan: good point. Maya, was the question still understandable to you, or did the raised brows change the meaning? I don't want to treat every difference in expression as a mistake if the sentence was readable.

Maya: I understood it from the context and the sign order, but without that context I might have read the whole phrase as a question. Your hands were easy to see, though. I was sitting near the window and the light wasn't great.

Rowan: that's useful to know. I'll prop the phone on the shelf instead of filming toward the window this week. I had the lamp behind me, which probably didn't help, and the video looks a little gray on my laptop too.

Priya: One small thing from the class recording: when you fingerspell “M-A-R-I-N,” you move the letters at slightly different heights. Maybe keep your wrist in one spot and let the handshape change. The name was still clear to me.

Rowan: thanks, Priya. I was more focused on getting the letters in order than keeping my hand steady. I'll do a few slow rounds before I record, but I won't speed them up until each shape feels comfortable.

Sam: For practice, I write the name on a card and put it beside the camera. That way I can check whether my fingerspelling matches the letters without looking down at my notes halfway through. It also keeps my shoulders from turning away.

Rowan: I like that. I usually put the word in my notebook below the phone, so I look down every couple of seconds. A card next to the lens might make the clip look less like I'm reading, even if I still need the reminder.

Maya: About the classifier in the middle, I liked that you showed the bus moving past the stop. I wasn't sure if you meant it went by without stopping or if it stopped farther down the road. Could you add the location in the setup?

Rowan: yes, I meant it went past without stopping. I see how the way I set it up could suggest it stopped somewhere else. I'll try marking the bus stop first, then show the bus passing it, rather than changing the movement itself.

Jules: That might help. When we did the neighborhood exercise, I placed the library and the corner store before I described the person walking between them. Otherwise everyone had to guess what my pointing referred to. I still mix up left and right when I'm facing the group.

Rowan: I do that too, especially when I watch myself mirrored on the screen. For now, I'll set up the two places and keep the camera view unmirrored while I practice. I'm not sure whether our class app saves the recording that way, so I'll check first.

Maya: Here are the three things I noticed, in order: 1) your hands stay in frame except for the last letter; 2) the question expression continues into the next phrase; 3) the bus location could be clearer. The first one is easy to fix by moving the phone back a little.

Rowan: thanks for writing it out like that. I can move the chair back instead of zooming out, since the phone was already using the wide setting. I'll try the expression pause and the bus setup separately, so I can tell what changed in each take.

Theo: I can lend you my little phone stand on Thursday if you want. It holds the phone higher than a stack of books, and the clamp doesn't cover the buttons. Just bring it back to the community room after the 6:30 class.

Rowan: that'd be great, thanks. I'll bring it back after class. I'm also going to ask Lena whether she can look at the second take, since she was the one who explained the question marker to our table last week.

Priya: Lena may be able to help, but give her a heads-up before class; she said she's helping set up the beginner tables on Thursday. You could send her the short clip instead of the whole five-minute practice, if she has time to look.

Nia — 10:23 am

Jordan — 10:34 am
